data.title: The Marcomanni and the Quadi – Germanic tribes north of the Roman Danube
data.excerpt: The Marcomanni came from the Main, and under Roman pressure they moved to Bohemia, where Maroboduus founded a powerful kingdom; the Quadi created a realm in what is today south-western Slovakia. The article follows their trade, crafts, burials and religion, from the gold bracelet in the princely grave at Zohor and the gravestone of the merchant Quintus Atilius Primus at Boldog to the Marcomannic Wars of Marcus Aurelius.
data.metaTitle: The Marcomanni and the Quadi – Germanic tribes on the Danube

children.text: The origin of the Germanic tribes of the Marcomanni and the Quadi

Our insights into the beginnings of the Germanic peoples, more precisely of the Marcomanni and the Quadi, come – as with other peoples – from prehistory. The first historically attested traces of Germanic peoples date from the 2nd century BC. The Marcomanni first appeared in the army of Ariovistus.

Their original settlement area lay on the Main, but under Roman pressure they migrated to Bohemia under the military leader Maroboduus shortly before the turn of the era. There they formed the centre of a tribal grouping. In the Marcomannic Wars the Romans managed to stabilise the northern frontier of their empire only with great effort. In the following centuries the Marcomanni continued to advance southwards. They are mentioned for the last time in the 4th century.

In antiquity the Germanic name was an ethnological generic term for a large group between the Celts and the Scythians. It was therefore primarily a name given from outside to certain peoples, and only to a lesser extent, and probably only secondarily, a name the Germanic peoples used for themselves.
Testimony of the ancient sources

Before Caesar's Gallic campaigns (58–52 BC) the peoples who had settled to the right of the Rhine remained largely outside the horizon of ancient observers, and when they did become known, they were at first regarded as Celts, or at least were not explicitly distinguished from them. The oldest historical reports on Germanic cultures come from encounters with the Greeks and the Roman Empire; the oldest written evidence, such as runic inscriptions, can be found only after the turn of the centuries.

The reports of ancient authors on the Germanic peoples are often based not on their own observations but on hearsay. As early as 330 BC the Greek traveller Pytheas of Massalia reported on the lands around the North Sea and the peoples living there.
Culture

The term Germani denotes linguistically related ancient tribes attested from the Iron Age (from the 6th century BC) in the north of Central Europe and in Scandinavia. The Germanic peoples did not form a homogeneous society as a nation.

The tribes of the Marcomanni and the Quadi were a society of warriors, craftsmen and farmers; there were layers of ruling princes and kings, of war leaders and also of slaves. Society was made up of the family, the district and the tribe. Not only the Marcomanni and the Quadi but all the Germanic tribes usually chose their commanders according to bravery and their king according to noble birth. Tacitus records the social system of the free Germanic men – ingenui – and of the aristocracy – nobilitas. Important and fundamental decisions were taken at the tribal assembly, attendance at which was a purely male affair. It can be assumed that the assembly had as many as a hundred members, and a majority decision was accepted.
3.1. Trade contacts

The gold bracelet from Zohor testifies to the lively trade contacts of the Germanic peoples with the Roman Empire. This gold bracelet, dated to the first and the beginning of the second century AD, is the most precious piece of jewellery of the Roman period discovered so far in the territory of present-day Slovakia, and it ranks among the rarest pieces of its kind in Europe as a whole.

The incomparably higher standard of living of the Romans also influenced the local Germanic elite. The gold bracelet from a rich princely grave at Zohor (Malacky district, south-western Slovakia) is proof of this. It probably belonged to a family or a lineage that controlled trade between the Roman Empire and the territory of present-day Slovakia in the 1st and 2nd centuries.

Crowds of Roman merchants poured into Maroboduus' kingdom to sell their goods here – among other things certainly some bronze vessels or jewellery. It is even reported that colonies of such merchants operated in Marcomannic territory. So far we have not discovered any of them, but the influx of Roman products is quite clear in graves and also at settlements of that time. Trade gave rise to the „profession“ of the negotiator, who specialised in transporting large consignments over long distances. Thanks to them Roman luxury goods found their way into Germanic and other non-Roman grave assemblages. They specialised in particular products (for example the negotiator olearius, the negotiator arits cretarie selling mainly terra sigillata, or the negotiator argentarius vascularius, who sold silver dining and drinking services, because ordinary tableware was not worth the trouble, and so on.) In certain cases a specialised producer and seller could be one and the same person. Trade often involved related material such as pottery, various metals and products made from them, jewellery, weapons, bronze and glass vessels, wine or oil. Combined trade also occurred. From the territory of the Barbaricum the Marcomanni and the Quadi exported to the Roman Empire agricultural produce (above all grain), cattle, furs, wool, amber and perhaps also slaves. Germanic exports to the Roman Empire were small compared with imports. Some sources mention, for example, the fair hair of Germanic women for the manufacture of wigs, but this claim is not yet archaeologically attested.
An important piece of evidence of trade in this period is the stele from Boldog:

children.text: The inscription is on a stone slab measuring 175 × 76 cm, which originally served as the gravestone of the Roman citizen Quintus Atilius Primus. In 1976 it was discovered by the administrator of the Roman Catholic parish during repairs to the church in Boldog.

It is the oldest Roman inscription discovered in Slovakia, as it dates from the 1st century AD. At first glance the inscription is brief, since it has only 11 lines, but it conceals unusually extensive information. Besides the name it contains biographical data on the deceased and his relatives, on their origin and on who had the gravestone made. The most important, however, is the information on the life career of Q. Atilius Primus. He was an officer, a centurion of the famous XV Legion garrisoned in the 1st century at Carnuntum, and at the same time, according to the interpretation of T. Kolník, he also held the post of interpreter to the legion, probably of both the Celtic and the Germanic language. After retiring he was a negotiator – a merchant. It is precisely in this information that the greatest historical value of the Boldog inscription lies.
The text of the inscription reads:
Q(uintus) Atilius
Sp(urii) f(ilius) Vot(uria tribu) Primus inter(p)rex mus interrex
[after Pichlerová and Neuman30] mus inter tre[x]
(cenarios)
leg(ionis) XV idem (centurio)
negotiator an(norum)
LXXX h(ic) s(itus) e(st)
Q(uintus) Atilius Cog(i)tatus Atilia Q(uinti) l(iberta) Fau
sta Privatus est
Martialis hered(es)
l(ibentes) p(osuerunt)

There is no doubt that Q. Atilius Primus built his career on the Amber Road. The economic and cultural development of the Germanic–Quadic occupation in what is today south-western Slovakia falls within the period of his military and commercial activity. The seat and main area of activity of Q. Atilius Primus was probably Carnuntum, an important transhipment point for goods at the crossroads of the Amber Road and the Danube route, even though his gravestone was reused at Boldog.
3. 2. Crafts

From Tacitus, and at the same time from Caesar, we have insights telling us that farming was not a favoured way of making a living among the Germanic peoples, yet archaeological finds tell us of long-term and regular cultivation of the land. Household work was left to women and children. Women held a highly esteemed position arising from natural respect and reverence.

One of the best attested economic activities is the extraction and working of iron – smelting and smithing. Altogether we now estimate the number of types of iron products manufactured at c. 40. The best known objects, which were placed in graves as grave goods, are for example spears, swords, iron components of shields and so on. Further tools usable also as weapons include axes and various knives. Various toilet razors, locks, keys, sheep shears and the like have also been found. Other interesting finds that we can attribute to the Marcomanni and the Quadi certainly include tongs, ploughshares, various scythes and sickles, awls, embossed vessels and cauldrons and so on.

The jewellery-making of the Marcomanni and the Quadi is regarded as masterly work. The finds comprise various items of jewellery, accessories and parts of dress. It was precisely during the existence of Maroboduus' realm that an extraordinary flowering of the second range of products – metal casting and the jeweller's art – began to appear throughout the Germanic world. Striking, massive brooches and belt clasps came into fashion and the production of decorative mounts for drinking horns spread. Some jewellery techniques stand out for their effectiveness and complexity, using contrasting openwork in sheet metal.

Besides the impressive evidence of metalworking there are many other productive activities that were carried on to varying extents among the Marcomanni as well as among the Quadi. Excavations at sites with favourable conditions for the preservation of wood and other organic materials often give us a range of products such as various kinds of wooden vessels, buckets, staffs, wooden weapons, furniture, boats and of course various architectural components. Various tools were used to work them. Finds attesting basketry have also come to light.

Archaeological finds give us evidence of the construction of pit kilns for firing pottery, and pottery production is also demonstrated by the enormous quantity of pottery sherds. In the period in question pottery was made by hand, without the use of the fast-rotating potter's wheel. The latter begins to appear among the Germanic peoples at the earliest at the end of the 2nd century AD. A peculiarity that distinguishes Germanic pottery of this period is rich decoration with impressions of a toothed wheel, which creates various contrasting patterns on the body of the vessel. The quality of the vessels differs between massive utility ware and fine tableware.
Products of bone and antler are also fairly numerous; we know, for example, antler combs, dress pins and also sewing needles. One of the most interesting finds of this period are bone gaming dice.
3. 3. The army

In the army probably only men fought; warrior graves that could be attributed to women have not yet been found from the period of the Marcomanni and the Quadi. A warrior was armed with a shield with a pointed central boss and with a spear, a sword and a knife. Initially long and heavy single-edged swords gradually became shorter, perhaps also under the influence of the short Roman sword – the gladius. Warriors not infrequently wore a mail shirt. Not infrequently a warrior also carried a small protective amulet.

The Marcomanni and also the Quadi, like the Germanic peoples in general, were often sought-after mercenaries for the Roman army. Germanic men were highly valued as soldiers of the auxiliary units but also as personal bodyguards. For their loyalty to the Romans and their part in the fighting against enemies they could even obtain land. Barbarians also penetrated into the highest command structures of the Roman army. Among the distinguishing marks of these soldiers were broad belts with bronze mounts, of which their owners were particularly proud. This belt was even placed in its owner's grave.

children.text: 3. 4. Burial

The funerary rite among the Germanic peoples was in most cases cremation. We also find evidence of ritual inhumation burials. Germanic graves of the nobility from the early Imperial period are inhumations and as a rule without weapons. Pottery or glass vessels, combs, brooches and buckles, and possibly other objects, served as grave goods placed in the graves – that is, artefacts similar to those in ordinary graves. Animals, for example a dog, or parts of them, for example horses' heads, could be used as grave goods.

The inhumation burials of the Suebi, which occur in certain phases of the Roman period at burial sites not only in Bohemia and Moravia but also in south-western Slovakia and Lower Austria, are quite varied (in both extended and crouched positions). The only criterion for identifying ritual burials on settlements, or in settlement pits, is the presence of grave goods.

The royal tomb near Mušov is a Germanic grave from the period of the Marcomannic Wars, situated near Mušov on the left bank of the River Dyje, not far from the Roman legionary fortress of Marcus Aurelius.

The tomb was discovered during excavations in 1988. Originally it was probably a hollow space whose timber structure collapsed. Although the tomb had been robbed in the past, it still contained around 200 Germanic and Roman objects of glass, silver, bronze and pottery, iron weapons, gold ornaments and many other objects testifying to the wealth of a Germanic ruler living in the vicinity of the Roman legions. Although the tomb dates from the 2nd century, the silver and gold funerary gifts are of earlier date. The oldest of them come from the late Republican or Augustan period, the more recent ones from roughly the years of the reigns of the emperors Tiberius and Nero, which shows that as early as the 1st century there existed in southern Moravia a trade in Roman luxury goods that passed from generation to generation among the local Germanic nobility. Such objects were probably brought directly from the Roman Empire as gifts to Germanic rulers, or became booty perhaps at the time of Vespasian's civil war, in which further Germanic warriors from the territory north of the Middle Danube also took part under their Germanic kings Italicus and Sido. Besides the funerary gifts the tomb contained the skeletal remains of sacrificial animals. According to anthropologists, the remains of two men and one woman were laid in the grave. It could therefore be the royal dynastic tomb of the Germanic ruler Ballomar from the period of the Marcomannic Wars, but evidence for this claim is lacking.
3. 5. Language

At present it is difficult to determine the exact pronunciation of the language used by the tribes of the Marcomanni and the Quadi. German dialects still contain many elements from this period today. The Germanic peoples left clear traces in the everyday vocabulary of standard German. Most of the Proto-Germanic words that have survived to the present day come from everyday life. For example, 2,000 years ago „bread“ was called „brauda“. In the 8th century the term „prōt“ was used and by the 11th century bread was called „brôt“. In today's German we translate the word for bread as das Brot.

Into the areas inhabited by the Marcomanni and the Quadi the Romans brought with them many things that were completely unknown to the Germanic peoples. The Germanic tribes, for example, built their houses as half-timbered structures, that is of wood and clay. Roman dwellings were of stone, as were the streets. Since there were no words for this in the Germanic languages, the local peoples adopted the Latin names. Thus the Roman „murus“ (a stone wall) became the Germanic word „mura“, our present-day múr (wall). In the same way our forebears Germanised „via layer“ (a paved road) into „strazza“, our present-day ulica (street), which today we translate into German as Die Strasse.
3. 6. Writing

Runes – the Germanic script was intended for special occasions rather than for everyday use. The name „runes“ is a term for the ancient characters, but we do not know what the Germanic peoples themselves called these signs. From the 3rd century the Elder Futhark was used; we know the phonetic values of the runes from later comparison with the Latin alphabet.
An inscribed cattle rib bone was found in 2017 in the Břeclav area and was studied in detail by a team of scientists from the Czech Republic, Austria, Switzerland and Australia.
3. 7. Housing

The Germanic peoples lived in relatively small hamlets. From the size of the cemeteries (cremation graves) of the Germanic tribes archaeologists infer that the size of the settlements was around two hundred people. Settlements only rarely developed according to a plan. Villages were often enclosed by a fence, rarely by a true palisade. Only in the frontier areas of the Roman Empire were villages protected and guarded by ramparts or palisades, once hostilities and mutual attacks began. Excavations show that the Germanic tribes lived in timber houses of frame construction. Since wood, unlike stone houses, rots in time, only archaeologically verifiable post holes tell us about the structure of the houses. The most widespread type was the three-aisled house, six to eight metres wide and often more than twice that in length, in individual cases over 60 m. Both the family and all the semi-free people and slaves fitted under its roof. The animals were separated off by a wall. The main advantage of this was that the animals helped to heat the house in the cold winter months. The living room had no further partitions and a fireplace stood in the middle. Smoke could escape through an opening in the roof. Germanic houses probably had no windows.
3. 8. Dress

The most typical male dress was a combination of trousers of various lengths and an upper shirt – a long-sleeved tunic. A very important part of male dress were of course the various decorated belts, two to a single costume. One was worn over the outer garment, with buckles, mounts and hanging ornaments; on the other, worn under the outer garment, objects of daily use such as knives, toilet implements or fire-steels were hung.

Thanks to finds of loom weights we know that fabrics were woven in various thicknesses. Among the materials, animal raw materials are known – wool, fur, leather. Of plant materials, flax or hemp was used. Among imports, silk was also used, as is suggested by finds from Mušov, for example. A very widely used item of clothing was the cloak or cape, fastened with a brooch at the shoulder. The number of brooches varies; the basic arrangement was two at the shoulders, and finds of three or four brooches, or of none at all, are not uncommon. It is probable that these brooches, like jewellery, spoke of the social standing of the wearer. (example: the size of a Germanic cloak 3 × 1.8 m)

Germanic men paid great attention to the care of their hair and beards. Besides iconographic depictions of Germanic men, finds of toilet implements from graves – combs, tweezers, shaving razors and the like – also tell of this. A complete picture of hair care and of the way the Suebian knot was tied is given, for example, by the head of a Germanic man on the bronze cauldron found in the princely grave at Mušov.
3. 9. Religion and myths
On the subject of the religion and myths of the Marcomanni and the Quadi we can again rely on the insights of Tacitus.

On the whole the religion of the Germanic peoples, across the chronological and cultural spheres of the individual Germanic peoples and tribal groups, is a polytheistic religion decentralised into local cult centres. It therefore seems reasonable to start from diverse, regionally differing cults rather than from a single unified concept.

With a great deal of caution we can name, in the pantheon of the Germanic gods, the supreme god, the god of war, the god of the weather and the goddess of fertility. Their names were Wodanaz/Wodan as the supreme god, Tý/Týr as the god of war and Tor/Donar as the god of the weather. The goddess of fertility was Nerthus, or Isis,
The Marcomanni

The Marcomanni were a Germanic people and formed part of the Suebian tribal confederation. They are first mentioned in the year 58 BC, when they were part of the army of Ariovistus. They lived in the Main region. In 9 BC the Roman commander Drusus attacked them and pushed them into the territory of present-day Bohemia, where their ruler Maroboduus founded a powerful „kingdom“ (a tribal confederation), the so-called realm of Maroboduus. Augustus declared the realm a threat to Rome. The Marcomanni took part in the wars of the Germanic peoples against the Roman Empire during the reign of Marcus Aurelius (166–180), which we call the Marcomannic Wars. In the 5th century, during the Migration Period, they left the territory of Bohemia and settled in present-day Bavaria.
4. 1. The area settled by the Marcomanni / Maroboduus' kingdom

Maroboduus demonstrated his political role in the year AD 9, when three whole Roman legions were massacred by the Germanic peoples under the leadership of Arminius in the Teutoburg Forest. Arminius was trying to unleash an uprising of the Germanic peoples and to drive the Romans out of Central Europe. He therefore offered Maroboduus the chance to join him in the war. Maroboduus, however, refused and decided to remain neutral. Once the Germanic uprising had essentially been defeated, Drusus Germanicus was recalled from Germania and Arminius could devote himself to inter-Germanic politics. He decided to take revenge on Maroboduus for not joining him in the war against Rome. In the year 17, together with his allies, he faced the Marcomanni and their associates in battle. The truth is that many tribes defected from Maroboduus to Arminius, because they probably understood his neutrality as cowardice and weakness. Although the battle ended indecisively, the tactical withdrawal of one of the wings of Maroboduus' army was regarded as a defeat, and the event was also politically exploited in this way by the leader of the Cherusci. Further tribes defected from Maroboduus. These events were crowned by the return of the Marcomannic magnate Catualda together with Gothic warriors, who drove Maroboduus out of Bohemia. He therefore fled with his retinue somewhere into the Middle Danube region, perhaps to Lower Austria or to south-western Slovakia, and there he begged the Romans for help against Catualda. They, however, refused and promised to secure protection for his person alone. He was then taken away and interned in Ravenna in northern Italy, where he lived for another eighteen years until his death in 37 or 38.

Maroboduus' retainers had to remain beyond the Danube and settled first in south-western Slovakia, where they became part of the vassal kingdom of Vannius. Catualda remained at the head of the Marcomanni for only a year; he was then overthrown by the Hermunduric king Vibilius and fled to beg the Romans for protection. He was interned in the town of Forum Iulium in Gallia Narbonensis. That was the end of Maroboduus' realm. The Marcomanni then disappear from the limelight of Roman politics and we hear of them more markedly again only at the time of the so-called Marcomannic Wars, which we date to the years 166–181.
The Quadi

The Quadi were a small Suebian tribe. They gained historical attention as allies of the Dacians, the Marcomanni and the Vandals in military conflicts with Rome and, in the Migration Period, in the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.
5.1. The area settled by the Quadi / the kingdom of Vannius

Vannius (AD 19–50), the first Quadic king known by name, was then appointed by Drusus the Younger as Roman client king of the Quadi and the Marcomanni. At the beginning of his reign he was loved and respected by the people, but later he became a tyrant.

In AD 50 Vannius' nephews (his sister's sons) Sido and Vangio allied against him with Vibillius, king of the Hermunduri. Vannius turned several times to the emperor Claudius, who refused him military support but instructed Publius Atellius Hister, the governor of Pannonia, to receive and protect Vannius. Vannius' forces (the Quadi as infantry and the Iazyges as cavalry) were too weak against his numerous enemies and so he entrenched himself in a fortified place. Wounded in the fighting, he had to flee with his adherents to the Danube, where ships were waiting. In Pannonia they were allotted land in the area of the Leitha Hills (present-day Austria). His nephews and successors Sido and Vangio shared the royal dignity and were loyal to the Romans. At first they were popular among the people, but they too developed into hated despots.

Especially in the second half of the reign of the emperor Valentinian I (364–375) the Pannonian Danube limes was very rapidly secured with a dense network of fortified posts and fortresses. Newly created ship anchorages in the Barbaricum guaranteed safe passage for Roman units in case of need. In addition, the Limes Sarmatiae was pushed forward opposite the province of Valeria on the eastern bank of the Danube. For this purpose the Romans, in breach of the treaty, annexed Quadic land, drove out the inhabitants and in 373 began to build a powerful fortress (the fort of Göd-Bócsaújtelep) beyond the new advanced frontier line, likewise on the tribal territory of the Quadi. The Quadic protests provoked by these measures led the level-headed and experienced commander of Valeria, Frigeridus, in coordination with his superior, to halt the construction. This in turn led to a game of intrigue in Rome, at the end of which Frigeridus was deposed in 373/374 and replaced by the inexperienced, arrogant Marcellianus. The new commander immediately had the building works resumed. At the same time the Quadic king Gabinius was invited to Valeria for talks on a false pretext and was treacherously stabbed at the end of the negotiations, his murderers showing no respect for the law of hospitality. Depending on the source (Zosimus and Ammianus Marcellinus), Celestius or Marcellianus himself was responsible for this deed. This led to a retaliatory campaign by the angry Quadi together with the Sarmatian tribe of the Iazyges, who had until then been regarded as Roman allies.

In June 374 Valentinian I fought against their raids into the Pannonian region and Moesia. The emperor set up his headquarters in the legionary camp of Brigetio (Komárom-Szőny). During the peace negotiations at Brigetio the emperor died on 17 November 375 after a stroke, which apparently came on in a fit of rage. The result of the Quadic–Sarmatian attack was that the works on the fortress of Göd-Bócsaújtelep, which had only recently begun again, were abruptly and this time definitively stopped and the Roman will to expand was suspended; all Roman control posts and measures, such as the Limes Sarmatiae to the east and north of the Pannonian Danube, were definitively abandoned.
Around the year AD 400 the Quadi came under the rule of the Huns.

In the territory of what is today south-western Slovakia, between the rivers Váh and Hron, the Quadi created a realm that lasted until the campaign of the Lombards into Italy (AD 568), which the Quadi joined. It is assumed that they were largely absorbed by the Lombards. Part of the Quadi were known in the 5th century as the Danubian Suebi and were absorbed by the Alamanni. The Suebi in Portugal may also have included remnants of the Quadi.
The Marcomannic Wars
The Marcomannic Wars are a series of wars that took place during the reign of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius between 166 and 180.

The wars were triggered by the numerous Sarmatian tribes, which invaded the Roman Empire from the north and were followed by the Germanic Marcomanni and Quadi. The attackers succeeded in breaking through the Roman defensive lines in the province of Pannonia (present-day Hungary), destroying the important military camps of Vindobona and Carnuntum, invading as far as northern Italy and surrounding the city of Aquileia.

Marcus Aurelius drove them back beyond the Danube and in 172 launched a massive offensive (expeditio Germanica prima). At the provincial capital of Carnuntum (between present-day Bratislava and Vienna) he built a pontoon bridge across the Danube and began a punitive expedition against the Germanic peoples. In view of the growing fighting strength of the Germanic peoples, the Romans prepared a total of 6 legions against the Marcomanni and their allies (1 legion consisted of 3,000–6,000 legionaries, but further auxiliary units must also be reckoned with). Three legions were to set out from Mainz on the Rhine (Slovak Mohuč) and another three from the area of Lower Austria, roughly from the surroundings of Vienna. Rome's plans were to join the forces of these legions inside Marcomannic territory and to defeat Maroboduus' armies with a single blow. This expedition penetrated deep into their territory and in a great battle defeated the more numerous army of the Sarmatians and the Quadi, with whom they finally concluded a peace treaty in 175.

Just two years later, however, the conflict was repeated and the Romans again defeated the Germanic peoples (expeditio Germanica secunda). An occupying army 40,000 strong remained in the originally Germanic territory and consideration was given to creating the provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia in the territory of today's Czech Republic and Slovakia. The plan was thwarted by the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius in 180, after which his successor, his son Commodus, ended the fighting and concluded a peace treaty with the Germanic tribes which temporarily restricted the independence of the individual tribes.
6.1. Phases of the Marcomannic Wars
– the attack of the barbarian tribes on the Roman Empire – the conflicts took place mostly in the territory of the empire
– the turn of the situation – the offensive of the Roman army against the strongest tribes (the Quadi, the Marcomanni and the Sarmatian Iazyges)
in 172 the Roman army crossed the Danube for the first time and defeated the Quadi, and a year later the Marcomanni as well
– after a short peace, renewed fighting; after the death of Marcus Aurelius his son and successor Commodus concluded peace with the Germanic peoples
when the fighting resumed in 177 the army operated deep in the territory of its opponents, and the well-known Roman inscription in Trenčín dates from this time (the winter of 179/180)
The first two phases are usually referred to as the First Marcomannic War, the third phase as the Second Marcomannic War.
Conclusion

The Marcomannic Wars revealed the weaknesses of the northern frontier of the Roman Empire, and as a result half of the Roman legions (16 out of a total of 33) were stationed along the Danube and the Rhine. For the Germanic tribes, although they were held back and defeated, the Marcomannic Wars were only the prelude to the great invasions that eventually broke up the Western Roman Empire completely and brought about its demise in the 4th and 5th centuries.
